newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Zaireans agree need for ceasefire, consult leaders.
newsitem.headline: Zaireans agree need for ceasefire, consult leaders.

text.p: Zaire's warring sides ended four days of peace talks in South Africa on Tuesday and said they agreed on the need for a ceasefire and democratic elections.

Delegates representing President Mobutu Sese Seko and rebel leader Laurent Kabila, who met for the first time in Pretoria on Saturday, issued a joint statement. But South African Deputy President Thabo Mbeki said they had to now consult their leaders.

"Both parties agreed on negotiations to bring about a peaceful, political solution to the conflict. This necessitates a complete cessation of hostilities and other measures consistent with the implementation of the U.N.-OAU peace plan," the statement said.

It gave no details of how or when a ceasefire might be implemented, but added: "The parties underlined the need for fundamental and democratic change...they concurred on the need for a process of transition leading to transparent, fair and inclusive elections."
The statement said such polls should be supervised by the international community. Both sides agreed Zaire should not be physically divided, it said.

Mbeki, who convened the talks along with Mohamed Sahnoun, representative of the United Nations and the Organisation of African Unity, told the news conference the Zaireans needed to consult their leaders.
"A spirit of mutual trust is developing...they are adjourning to allow the parties to consult their principals," Mbeki said.
He said the parties had discussed the "timing and modalities" of a ceasefire.

After Mbeki read out the joint statement, rebel delegate Bizima Karaha said: "We learnt a lot from what happened here and we shall take our process forward...There were more common points than divergences."

Karaha said his government counterpart, Foreign Minister Kamanda wa Kamanda, also wanted democracy and human rights for all. "The most important thing is that we have entered in the train, the train is moving and we are all aboard."
Kamanda wa Kamanda described the talks as "profound".
"Thanks to the work that has been done here we are entering in a dynamic process which is supported by a perception of the problems that have to be solved," he said.
The Zaireans left the news conference without taking questions. It was not immediately clear when they would head back to Zaire.
In Zaire, Kabila said his fighters had reached a town only 270 km (170 miles) northeast of the capital Kinshasa.
"We are in Kasai Oriental. Elements have arrived in Bandundu and Mbandaka," Kabila said without elaborating.

But in Zaire's second city of Lubumbashi, diehard soldiers in Mobutu's collapsing army said they had driven back a rebel advance on the copper city. It was rocked by explosions overnight but was peaceful during the day.
Zaire's parliament in Kinshasa was shut for a second day as militant supporters of Prime Minister Etienne Tshisekedi disrupted lawmakers' plans to remove him.
